sections.title: Cap and form
sections.text: Mycena rosea, the rosy bonnet, is a small to medium agaric. Its cap is about 2.5–7 cm across, convex at first and later flattening, often with a low central umbo. The smooth, waxy-looking surface is hygrophanous: pink to lilac-pink, it pales as it dries or ages and may develop a yellowish centre. The margin is finely translucent-striate.

sections.title: Gills, stem and flesh
sections.text: The gills are pale white to pink, moderately spaced, ventricose and ascending; they are notched near the stem and may become interveined with age. The stem is usually 6–10 cm long, hollow, whitish to pale pink, often widened toward the base and covered there with whitish, sometimes yellowish, fibrils. The flesh is thin and white, with a distinct radish-like smell. The spore print is white.

sections.title: Habitat and identification
sections.text: It grows singly or scattered in leaf litter in broadleaf woods, especially beneath beech and oak, and sometimes in mixed woods; it is mainly found in autumn. Mycena pura is a close look-alike. The more uniform pink colour and often more robust stature can help, but the characters overlap and do not always provide a reliable macroscopic distinction; microscopy and the full character set may be needed.

sections.title: Safety
sections.text: This species is regarded as toxic and must not be eaten. Some guides place it among muscarinic-type poisonings; however, the Université Lyon 1 account states that M. rosea contains no muscarine and mentions other possible compounds. The responsible toxin is therefore not presented here as established. If ingestion occurs, contact a poison centre or emergency services immediately.

traits: Pink to lilac-pink cap, 2.5–7 cm wide, often low-umbonate, hygrophanous and translucent-striate at the margin; it pales as it dries
White to pink, ventricose, ascending gills, notched near the stem; white spore print
Hollow whitish to pale-pink stem, often widened and fibrillose at the base
Thin white flesh with a radish-like smell
Leaf litter in broadleaf woods, especially beneath beech or oak; mainly an autumn mushroom
